speaker: fitz
text: Hidden inside Hoover Dam are more than five hundred and eighty miles of pipe.

speaker: fitz
text: One-inch steel pipe, sealed into the concrete. Why would anyone bury plumbing inside a dam?

speaker: gauge
text: Did someone forget to take the plumbing out? I brought a wrench.

speaker: fitz
text: Nobody forgot. To solve it, we go back to a river that wouldn't behave.

speaker: gauge
text: New case. Gauge's Fix-It List, volume two.

speaker: fitz
text: What happened to volume one?

speaker: gauge
text: The wind took it.

speaker: fitz
text: The Colorado River used to swing between floods and low water, carrying huge loads of silt.

speaker: fitz
text: California's Imperial Valley, below sea level, watered its farms with a canal from the river.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1904, silt clogged the canal, so the canal company cut a quick, temporary bypass, with no control gates.

speaker: gauge
text: No gates? So nothing to shut it with?

speaker: fitz
text: Nothing. In 1905, floods tore it open, and most of the river poured toward a low, dry basin.

speaker: fitz
text: It wrecked farms, railroads and roads, and the water in the basin became the Salton Sea.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number one. Build a taller canal wall.

speaker: fitz
text: A wall wasn't the problem. The river was. Even low dams wouldn't have done much against floods like that. It needed one very high dam.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number one, upgraded.

speaker: fitz
text: It would also store water and make power. In 1922, seven states signed a deal on sharing the river.

speaker: fitz
text: The Bureau of Reclamation, the agency that designed the dam, chose Black Canyon.

speaker: fitz
text: It was narrow, about three hundred feet wide at the river, so cheaper to fill. The rock was solid.

speaker: gauge
text: Black Canyon? Isn't it the Boulder Canyon Project?

speaker: fitz
text: The name came from earlier legislation, and it stuck.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number two. Just build the dam right in the river.

speaker: fitz
text: You can't pour concrete into a fast river. So first, they moved it.

speaker: fitz
text: Crews blasted four tunnels, two through each canyon wall, each dug fifty-six feet across and lined down to fifty.

speaker: gauge
text: Fifty feet across? That's not a tunnel. That's a hallway for giants.

speaker: fitz
text: In November 1932, they blocked the old channel with rock and earth, and the river turned into the tunnels.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix two, detoured.

speaker: fitz
text: Then two earth-and-rock walls, called cofferdams, closed off the site, upstream and downstream, and it was pumped dry.

speaker: fitz
text: By Reclamation's figures, the upstream one was seven hundred and fifty feet thick at its base.

speaker: gauge
text: Thicker than the dam?

speaker: fitz
text: At the bottom, yes. And remember the downstream one. It comes back later.

speaker: gauge
text: Clue one.

speaker: fitz
text: Meanwhile, high scalers on ropes cleared loose rock off the cliffs with jackhammers and dynamite.

speaker: fitz
text: Up there, the danger came from above: falling rock and dropped tools. So some men coated cloth hats in coal tar: hard-boiled hats.

speaker: gauge
text: Hard-boiled. Like an egg. A very tough egg.

speaker: fitz
text: Then the company handed real hard hats to every man, one of the first big projects to do that.

speaker: fitz
text: Deep in the Great Depression, about twenty-one thousand men worked on the dam over the years.

speaker: fitz
text: The workers' town wasn't ready, so families camped by the river in tents and cardboard shelters. People called it Ragtown.

speaker: fitz
text: Summer hit about a hundred and twenty degrees.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number three. Ice. For everybody.

speaker: fitz
text: The workers asked for something like that.

speaker: fitz
text: The builders, a group of firms called Six Companies, had a boss on the job, Frank Crowe, known as "Hurry-Up Crowe."

speaker: fitz
text: In August 1931, the company moved some tunnel workers to lower-paid jobs. Within hours, everyone went on strike.

speaker: fitz
text: They asked for clean water, flush toilets, ice water on the job, and for the state mining laws to be followed.

speaker: gauge
text: They asked first.

speaker: fitz
text: Crowe turned down every demand, and after about a week the men went back. But afterward, water, lighting and housing got better.

speaker: fitz
text: Black workers were barred from living in the government's new town, Boulder City. And according to PBS, by 1933 they were less than one percent of the workforce.

speaker: fitz
text: Building the dam cost lives. Officially, ninety-six men died: men killed in accidents at the dam site.

speaker: gauge
text: Officially?

speaker: fitz
text: The count leaves out deaths from heat, pneumonia, and heart trouble.

speaker: fitz
text: In the summer of 1931, Reclamation's records list sixteen people who died of the heat, even women in the camps. None are in the ninety-six.

speaker: fitz
text: In the tunnels, exhaust from gasoline trucks made men sick. Company doctors called it pneumonia. Historians still argue how many of the pneumonia deaths were really carbon monoxide.

speaker: fitz
text: Reclamation says the record "is just not that clear." Historians say the real number is higher.

speaker: fitz
text: A plaque by the sculptor Oskar Hansen remembers them. It begins, "They died to make the desert bloom."

speaker: gauge
text: People say some workers are buried inside the concrete. Is that true?

speaker: fitz
text: No. Reclamation says plainly that no one is buried in Hoover Dam.

speaker: fitz
text: The concrete went in five feet at a time. Each bucket raised it only a few inches, while several men spread it and watched.

speaker: fitz
text: And there's one family in these records. Years before the dam was approved, a Reclamation surveyor, J. G. Tierney, drowned in the river while scouting sites, on December twentieth.

speaker: fitz
text: The last man on the official list is his son, Patrick. He died in a fall from an intake tower, on December twentieth, 1935. The same date.

speaker: gauge
text: Ninety-six on the list, and more who aren't. I'll remember them all.

speaker: fitz
text: Now, the shape. From above, the dam curves out toward the lake.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number four. Make it a straight wall. Same thickness all the way up. Simple.

speaker: fitz
text: Water pushes harder the deeper it gets. At the bottom, Reclamation says, about forty-five thousand pounds on every square foot.

speaker: fitz
text: So the dam is six hundred and sixty feet thick at the bottom, and just forty-five at the top.

speaker: gauge
text: Six hundred and sixty feet?

speaker: fitz
text: Remember how thick it is.

speaker: gauge
text: Clue two.

speaker: fitz
text: It's an arch-gravity dam. Gravity: it weighs more than six point six million tons, so its weight pins it to the rock.

speaker: fitz
text: Arch: the curve works like a stone arch on its side. The lake squeezes it into the canyon walls, and the rock pushes back.

speaker: gauge
text: So which one really holds the water? The weight, or the curve?

speaker: fitz
text: Reclamation says both. But the historians Billington and Jackson, quoted by the National Park Service, say the base is so massive that the designers "neglected to make essential use of the arch effect."

speaker: gauge
text: So my straight wall was right?

speaker: fitz
text: Your thin straight wall? No. The heavy part? Yes.

speaker: gauge
text: Half right. I'm framing that.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number five. A dam this big needs decoration. Eagles. Lots of eagles.

speaker: fitz
text: Reclamation's engineers wanted eagles, and cornices too. The architect Gordon Kaufmann took the ornament off and left the great curved face plain.

speaker: fitz
text: Reclamation's engineers designed the structure. He designed the look.

speaker: gauge
text: Goodbye, eagles. You were majestic.

speaker: fitz
text: Around Hansen's two thirty-foot bronze figures, a star map shows the sky on the evening of the dedication, September thirtieth, 1935.

speaker: fitz
text: The dam sits on a state line, and a time-zone line. The Nevada side is on Pacific time. The Arizona side is on Mountain time.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number six. Pick one time zone.

speaker: fitz
text: Nevada uses daylight saving time, and most of Arizona has skipped it since 1968. So in summer, their clocks match. In winter, Arizona is an hour ahead.

speaker: gauge
text: Two watches. Fix six, done.

speaker: fitz
text: President Franklin Roosevelt began his dedication speech, "This morning I came, I saw and I was conquered." But he called it Boulder Dam.

speaker: gauge
text: Wait. It changed names too?

speaker: fitz
text: Hoover in 1930. Boulder in 1933, by order of the new Interior Secretary. Hoover again in 1947, from Congress and President Truman.

speaker: gauge
text: Hoover, Boulder, Hoover. It's a dam, not a tennis ball.

speaker: fitz
text: When the lake gets too high, water goes over the spillways and down huge tunnels in the rock.

speaker: fitz
text: They've been used only twice: in 1941, when the lake first filled, and in 1983.

speaker: fitz
text: The water can hit about a hundred and twenty miles per hour.

speaker: gauge
text: Is fast bad?

speaker: fitz
text: At that speed, a small bump drops the pressure so low that cold water boils into tiny bubbles. When they collapse, they hammer the concrete. That's cavitation.

speaker: gauge
text: Bubbles can chew concrete? I've been underestimating bubbles.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1941, it tore a hole in the Arizona tunnel. About a hundred and fifteen feet long, thirty wide and forty-five deep.

speaker: fitz
text: The most probable cause, Reclamation's engineers said, was a small hump in the floor.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number seven. Make the concrete smoother.

speaker: fitz
text: That was the 1940s plan. They rebuilt it and polished it smooth. It helped, but it wasn't enough on its own.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1983 the damage was minor, but the engineers warned that this kind of damage adds up. So in the mid-1980s, they added a fix that sounds backwards.

speaker: fitz
text: A ramp and slot called an aerator mixes air into the water next to the concrete. The bubbles collapse into a cushion of air, not the wall.

speaker: gauge
text: The fix for bubbles was more air. Smoother: not enough.

speaker: gauge
text: Didn't Hoover Dam nearly fail in 1983?

speaker: fitz
text: That's a mix-up. Reclamation's engineers contrasted Hoover's minor damage with the extensive damage at Glen Canyon Dam, upstream.

speaker: fitz
text: Lake Mead has been near record lows. Reclamation says that below about one thousand and thirty-five feet, the older turbines are expected to suffer severe cavitation damage.

speaker: fitz
text: So five of the seventeen have been refitted as wide-head turbines, built for a much wider range of levels.

speaker: gauge
text: Same enemy. Bubbles, again.

speaker: fitz
text: Which brings us back to the pipes. Concrete heats up as it sets. In a mass this big and thick, the heat gets trapped.

speaker: gauge
text: Final fix. Pour it all in one go, and wait for it to cool.

speaker: fitz
text: Reclamation's engineers calculated that poured as one solid block, it would have taken about a hundred and twenty-five years to cool.

speaker: gauge
text: A hundred and twenty-five years?

speaker: fitz
text: And as it cooled, it would have shrunk, and cracked.

speaker: fitz
text: So they built it as about two hundred and fifteen columns of blocks, poured five feet at a time.

speaker: fitz
text: Inside each layer, they laid loops of one-inch steel pipe. More than five hundred and eighty miles in all.

speaker: fitz
text: First they ran river water through them. Then ice-cold water, from a refrigeration plant on the downstream cofferdam.

speaker: gauge
text: The downstream wall. So the dam had air conditioning. Well, water conditioning.

speaker: fitz
text: As each block cooled, its pipes were cut off and filled with grout. Grout went into the gaps between the columns too, so the dam acts as one piece. Cooling was finished in March 1935.

speaker: gauge
text: So I can't take the plumbing out?

speaker: fitz
text: It's not plumbing anymore. It's part of the dam.

speaker: gauge
text: I'll find another pipe.

speaker: gauge
text: So is it still curing? Soft in the middle?

speaker: fitz
text: Not soft, no. But like most concrete, it has kept very slowly gaining strength for decades.

speaker: fitz
text: So why is Hoover Dam full of pipes? Because poured as one solid block, it would have taken more than a century to cool, and it would have cracked.

speaker: gauge
text: Volume two survived. Mostly.

speaker: fitz
text: One fix half right.

speaker: gauge
text: Half right. My best case yet.

speaker: gauge
text: Ooh, what else is built weird? Subscribe and let's find out.
